en: Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhi of Changshui, Part Two:

Refuting the Six Entrances (*ṣaḍāyatana*). In Sanskrit, this is *praveśa*, which here is translated as "entrance" (*rù*) or "locus" (*chù*), because it is the locus where objects enter, and also because it is the place where consciousness arises.
Now, both dharmas—the sense faculties and their objects—are...

Regarding the locus where consciousness arises, it is now analyzed by dividing it into the six sense organs (*indriya*) and refuting them individually; therefore, the sense organs alone are taken as the "entrances" (*āyatana*).
The text has two parts:
first, a general inquiry.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
What is the nature of the six sense bases as the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous true suchness?
It is to be understood in the same manner as the initial explanation of the five aggregates."
2. Specific Refutation, in six parts:
1. The Sense-base of the Eye, in three parts:
1. Indicating its lack of intrinsic nature, in two parts:
1. Illustrating Delusion through a Simile: "Ānanda!
That very act of staring with the eyes until they become weary—both the eyes and the weariness—are equally the signs of the delusive exhaustion produced by staring within Bodhi."
This borrows from the previous section on the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), using the metaphor of staring at flowers with fixed eyes.
The pupils of the eyes represent the nature of awakening (bodhi-svabhāva); "staring until fatigue arises" represents the sudden emergence of deluded thoughts (vikalpa).

Furthermore, regarding the eyes and the resulting fatigue: it is this very faculty of the eye that acts as both the binder and the bound. Since its arising does not depart from the Truth, it is said that they are equally Bodhi. The wording of the sutra is abbreviated;

if one were to discuss it in detail, the pure eyes would metaphorically represent the nature of awakening (*bodhicitta*). The fatigue produced by staring represents ignorance (*avidyā*), which, due to a lack of understanding, gives rise to discursive thought and movement. Because this fatigue arises, one sees flowers in the air; this metaphorically represents how, due to the movement of discursive thought, false objects and the sense-faculties (the body) manifest.
The phrase "both the eyes and mental toil" uses a metaphor to indicate the Dharma.

"Eyes" refers to the movement of ignorance (*avidyā*), while "mental toil" refers to the manifested sense organs and objects, as well as the perceiving mind. These mental objects and the stirring thoughts are both the characteristics of the toil of ignorance within the nature of the Bodhisattva; they have no substantial essence that can be found, arising falsely like seeing flowers in the sky when staring with fixed eyes—both are merely toil.
2. Distinguishing Non-existence with Respect to Objects:
"Based on the two kinds of delusory objects—light and darkness—the faculty of vision arises within them; it absorbs these objective images, and this is called the nature of seeing."
"This seeing is ultimately without substance apart from those two objects, light and darkness.

Since these delusive realms manifest due to the movement of the mind, they branch out within these delusive realms as sense organs and objects; they exist in mutual opposition, established through reciprocal definition. They originally possess no self-nature, and their substance cannot be apprehended.

The subsequent text states: "Cognition is triggered by objects, and appearances arise because of the sense organs; yet both appearance and seeing lack inherent nature, like two reeds leaning against each other.
Therefore, it says that through light and darkness, seeing is activated and resides within them.

When dust arises, it stimulates the sense organ; the organ, in turn, perceives the object. Only when both organ and object are present is the nature of seeing established; thus it is said that "sucking this in is called the nature of seeing," and so forth.
Since it is by virtue of perceiving an object that it acquires the name "seeing," one knows that this seeing arises from the reflected image.
"Images" (xiàng) are metaphors for sensory objects (*viṣaya*).

The *Awakening of Faith* states: "Just as a bright mirror manifests forms and images, so too does the manifesting consciousness (*nirbhāsa-vijñāna*); as each of the five sense-objects arrives before it, they are immediately manifested."
"Since even light and darkness are like reflections, having no substantiality that can be apprehended, how much less could the seeing that arises from them have any substantiality?
Therefore, it is said that apart from those [objects], there is no substance.
Second, the refutation of the formation of non-characteristics has two parts:
1. Marking Non-arising:
"In this way, Ānanda!
You should know that this seeing does not come from light or darkness; it does not emerge from the sense organ; nor is it produced from space."

Although the preceding text spoke of [the sense organs] being caused by light and darkness, this was to reveal that the nature of the faculties is fundamentally non-existent and exists only in dependence upon others; it appears to have causes only from the perspective of deluded discrimination.
Now, by investigating through these four points, one finds that its essence has no place of arising; this is why it is so designated.
Second, the refutation of the place of arising:
"For what reason?"
If it comes from light, then darkness would be extinguished along with it, and thus one should not see darkness.
If it comes from darkness, then light would be extinguished along with it, and thus one should not see light.
If it were produced from the sense organ, there would necessarily be neither light nor darkness;
thus, this essence of vision would fundamentally lack its own inherent nature.
If it emerged from empty space, then when it gazes forward at external forms, it should return to see the sense organ itself.
Furthermore, when emptiness observes itself, how does it concern your entry?

First, regarding the arising from the object: within the object itself, light and darkness are mutually exclusive; because of light, one does not see darkness, for at the time of darkness there is no light, and seeing follows the cessation of light. Because of darkness, the opposite occurs.

Next, the arising of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) is refuted: the arising of the sense-faculties does not depend upon light and darkness; since light and darkness do not come [to them], the sense-faculties lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Here, the term "arising of the sense-faculties" refers to the faculty in relation to itself, and does not mean the refutation of consciousness (*vijñāna*); alternatively, it may refer to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) in relation to the conventional sense-faculties (*saṃvṛti-satya*), hence the expression "arising of the sense-faculties."

Next, I shall refute the notion that space gives rise [to perception]. If you claim that space can produce [perception] such that the ultimate reality resides within the floating dust, then when advancing, one should observe the image, and when retreating, one should observe the sense organ.
Furthermore, if space itself inherently possesses the capacity for seeing, what concern is this with your own visual faculty?
3. Conclusion on Falsity:
"Therefore, you should know that the eye-faculty is false; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
This is to be understood as explained previously.
II. The Ear-entrance (śrotra-āyatana), in three parts:
1. Designating its lack of substantiality, in two parts:
A. Citing a metaphor to reveal its falsity.

“Ānanda! It is like a person who blocks their ears tightly with two fingers; because the faculty of hearing is strained, sounds arise within the head. Both the ear and the strain are, in fact, the signs of fatigue produced by the fixed gaze of Bodhi.”
The ear is a metaphor for true nature, and the hand is a metaphor for ignorance; the union of the true and the delusive is called "obstruction.
The initial stirring of thought is called "exhaustion"; because thought stirs, objects appear, just as sound arises from the head.

Furthermore, the ears and their associated fatigue—these moving thoughts and delusive objects, as well as the objects manifested by the mind that binds them—are all the signs of ignorance and weariness within the nature of Bodhi.
In this context, "staring" refers to both the act of blocking the ears and the act of gazing straight ahead; hence it is also called "staring.
Second, the absence [of self-nature] is distinguished in relation to objects:
"Based on the two kinds of false objects—movement and stillness—the faculty of hearing arises within the center; it draws in these objective images, which is termed the nature of listening."
This hearing, when separated from the two objects of movement and stillness, ultimately lacks any substance.

Since the object triggers the faculty and the faculty in turn perceives the object, hearing can only be established through the mutual dependence of faculty and object; therefore, this ear-faculty has no substance when separated from its object.
2. Refuting [the notion of] establishment to demonstrate signlessness, in two parts:
1. Indicating non-arising:
"In this way, Ānanda!"
"You should know that this hearing does not come from movement or stillness, nor does it emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from space.
Second, the refutation of the place of production: "Why is this so?"
If it comes from stillness, then movement would immediately cease along with it, and one should not perceive movement.
If it comes from movement, then stillness would immediately cease along with it, and one should have no awareness of stillness.
If it were produced from the sense organ, it would necessarily be devoid of movement and stillness.
Thus, the essence of hearing fundamentally lacks intrinsic nature.
If it emerged from space and possessed the nature of hearing, it would no longer be empty space.
Furthermore, if emptiness hears by itself, how does it concern your faculty of hearing?

First, one must refute the arising [of hearing] from the object. Since objects possess movement and stillness, one would hear one thing but not hear another, because hearing follows that which can produce it, and thus possesses arising and ceasing.
Next, the arising from the sense organs is refuted, because if it were so, there would likewise be no hearing when movement and stillness are absent.

Finally, the arising from space is refuted: if space itself possessed hearing, it would constitute a sense organ in its own right; furthermore, if space were to hear by itself, how could it possibly involve the ear?
3. Conclusion on Falsity:
"Therefore, you should know that the ear-faculty is false; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
3. The Nose-faculty (Ghrāṇāyatana), Part Three:
First, indicating that it has no substantial reality, in two parts:
first, citing a metaphor to reveal its falsity.
"Ānanda!..."

For example, suppose there is a person who forcefully pinches their nose; after pinching it for a long time, they become fatigued and perceive a sensation of cold within the nose. Based on that sensation, they distinguish between what is open or obstructed, and what is real or unreal, extending even to various fragrant and foul odors.
"Furthermore, the nose and labor are both manifestations of the exhaustion produced by the staring of Bodhi.
The nose is a metaphor for true nature; the external wind is a metaphor for ignorance (*avidyā*).
"Holding" refers to the contraction of the breath, which is a metaphor for the union of the true and the false.
"Exertion" (*lao*) is a metaphor for the movement of the mind; "cold touch," "fragrance," and "stench" are metaphors for delusory objects.
The rest of the text is as before.
Second, distinguishing non-existence through the ultimate object.
"Based upon the two kinds of false objects—openness and obstruction—the faculty of hearing arises within them; it inhales these objective images, which is called the nature of smelling and hearing.
This hearing, apart from those two objects of openness and obstruction, ultimately has no substance."
The explanation of "Śākya" is as in the preceding text.
Second, the refutation of the establishment of signlessness has two parts:
first, the indication of non-arising.

"You should know that this hearing does not come from the openness or closure, nor does it emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced in space; neither in the openness, the closure, the sense organ, nor in space is there a place of origin.
2. Refuting the Place of Origin.
"Why is this? If [the sense of hearing] comes from openness, then when it is obstructed, the hearing ceases; how then could one know the obstruction?
If it exists because of obstruction, then when there is openness, there would be no hearing; how then could it manifest the perception of fragrances, odors, and other tactile sensations?"
If it arose from the sense organ, there would necessarily be no alternation between openness and obstruction.
Thus, the faculty of hearing would inherently lack self-nature.

If it emerged from space, then that hearing would naturally turn back to smell your own nose; since space itself would possess the power of hearing, what connection would it have with your auditory faculty?
First, the arising [of consciousness] from the object is refuted; the mutual refutation of "passage" and "obstruction" can be understood through this.
"To manifest" means to clarify.

Next, the arising [of consciousness] from the sense organ is refuted: if it arises from the sense organ, there would be no object; if there is no object, there would be no sense organ, because cognition is triggered by the sensory field (*viṣaya*).
The faculty (organ) is also a root.

Next, I shall refute the notion that space gives rise to [smell]. Previously, it was the object of hearing; now, it is reduced to the root of smelling. If space itself smells the fragrance, what use is your nose?
3. Conclusion on Falsity:
"Therefore, one should know that the nose-faculty is false; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
4. The Tongue-faculty (jihvā-āyatana), in three parts:
First, indicating that it has no substantial reality, in two parts:
first, citing a metaphor to reveal its falsity.
"Ānanda!..."

For example, suppose there is a person who licks their lips with their tongue; as they lick repeatedly until it becomes fatigued, if that person is ill, they will perceive a bitter taste, whereas a healthy person will experience a slight sensation of sweetness.

Through sweetness and bitterness, this neutral flavor of the tongue-root is revealed to be ever-present when it is unmoving; thus, both the tongue and its fatigue are equally the appearance of *bodhi* manifesting as a state of exhaustion.
The unmoving tongue-root is a metaphor for the True; the lips are a metaphor for Ignorance; and licking is a metaphor for the union of the True and the delusory.
"Exertion" refers to the movement of thought; because thought moves, objects arise, such as sweetness, bitterness, or blandness.
Question:
Sweetness and bitterness arise from exertion and can thus be used as metaphors for delusory objects.
Salivation occurs when the tongue-organ is unmoving; this may appropriately be compared to the True [Nature]. Why, then, is it used as a metaphor for an object?
Answer:
Originally, immovability can be used as a metaphor for the Real; however, now that immovability is manifested by means of movement, it becomes a relative concept, and thus it constitutes delusion.
As it says below: "Words of falsehood reveal all that is true; yet both falsehood and truth are equally false.
The rest is as in the text.
Second, [the section] on revealing non-existence by means of objects.
"Based on the two kinds of false objects—sweetness, bitterness, and blandness—a cognition arises within, which inhales these objective images; this is called the nature of the sense of taste.
This nature of the sense of taste, when separated from those three objects of sweetness, bitterness, and blandness, ultimately has no substance."
2. Refuting [the notion of] establishment to demonstrate signlessness, in two parts:
1. Indicating non-arising:
"In this way, Ānanda!"

"You should know that this perception of bitter and bland taste does not come from sweetness or bitterness, nor does it exist because of blandness, nor does it emerge from the sense organ, nor is it produced from empty space.
Second, the refutation of the place of production.
"Why is this? If sweetness or bitterness arises, then neutrality is known to cease; how, then, can one know neutrality?
If one emerges from neutrality, then sweetness is known to perish; how, furthermore, can one know the two characteristics of sweetness and bitterness?"
If it were produced from the tongue, there would necessarily be no objects of sweetness, blandness, or bitterness;
thus you know that the root of tasting has no intrinsic nature.
If it emerged from space, then space itself would have the taste, and it would not be known by your mouth.
Furthermore, emptiness knows itself; what does it have to do with your sense-faculties?
Whether considered from the perspective of the object, the faculty, or emptiness itself, the explanation is as before.
Regarding "emptiness tasting itself," "taste" (wei) refers to the act of tasting.
3. Conclusion on Falsity:
"Therefore, you should know that the tongue-sphere is false; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
5. The Body-Sphere (kāyāyatana), three parts:
First, indicating that it has no substantial reality, in two parts:
first, citing a metaphor to reveal its falsity.
"Ānanda!..."

For example, suppose a person touches a hot hand with a cold hand: if the power of the cold is greater, the hot hand follows the cold; if the efficacy of the heat prevails over the cold, it becomes hot.

Thus, by means of this contact of combined perception, the cognition of separation is manifested; when the momentum is established, it arises from the contact of fatigue. Both the body and the fatigue are, in fact, the signs of fatigue produced by the *bodhi* (enlightened mind) itself through its own staring.
The two hands are a metaphor for the true and the false; their joining is a metaphor for the union of the true and the false.

The true nature does not maintain its own essence but follows conditions to form the sense organs, objects, and so forth, just as the hands become cold or hot depending on the conditions of cold or heat.
Question:
Between the two hands, which hand is used as the metaphor for the Real?
Answer:
Contemplate this by using those with inferior power as an analogy for the ultimate truth.
The rest is as stated in the text.
Second, the absence [of objects] is distinguished in relation to sensory objects (*viṣaya*).
"Based on the two kinds of false objects—the separated and the combined—the faculty of awakening arises in the midst of them, absorbing these objective images; this is called the nature of cognition.
Yet, this essence of cognition, when separated from those two objects of separation and combination, as well as opposition and compliance, ultimately has no inherent substance."
2. Refuting [the notion of] production to establish signlessness, in two parts:
1. Indicating non-arising:
"Thus it is, Ānanda!"

"You should know that this awakening does not come from separation or union, nor does it exist through opposition or conformity; it does not emerge from the sense organs, nor is it produced from empty space.
2. Refuting the place of its arising.
"Why is this? If [the mind] comes when there is conjunction, it must have already ceased when there is separation; how then could one perceive separation?
The same applies to the two characteristics of opposition and compliance."

If it emerged from the sense organs, there would necessarily be no separation or union; thus, the four phases of attraction and aversion would be known by your body-consciousness alone, which would fundamentally lack its own inherent nature.
If it emerged from space, then space itself would possess cognition and awareness; what connection would that have to your faculties?
The arising from the breaking of objects further elaborates upon the principles of the two aspects—contradiction and conformity—following the same pattern of separation and combination as before.
The subsequent arisings from the sense-faculties and from space are both as stated in the text.
3. Conclusion on Falsity:
"Therefore, one should know that the sense-base of the body is false; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
6. The Sense-Base of the Mind (manāyatana), three parts:
First, indicating that it has no substantial reality, in two parts:
first, citing a metaphor to reveal its falsity.
"Ānanda!..."
"For example, when a person is weary they fall asleep; having slept soundly, they awaken. When they encounter sensory objects, they remember them; losing this memory constitutes forgetfulness.
Here, "person" is a metaphor for the true nature (*tathatā*), because it is inherently awakened from the beginning.
Fatigue leading to sleep is a metaphor for ignorance deluding the truth, because its nature is not clearly understood.
Deep sleep is a metaphor for the manifestation of objects through the movement of thought; that is to say, because one sleeps, dreams are formed, and dreams possess both mind and objects.
The mind is likened to the transformation of karma (*karmavipāka*), and the object is likened to the manifested appearance.

Awakening is likened to the phenomenal consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*); this phenomenal consciousness grasps the manifested objects, discriminating between the defiled and the pure. Failing to realize that these are manifestations of one's own mind, it perceives them as coming from the outside. This is like recollecting events from a dream, which cannot be clearly perceived; hence it is said, "surveying the sensory objects, one recalls them."
Losing memory means forgetting.

"This refers to the inverted states of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing; they are absorbed and practiced within, returning without transgressing one another, which is called the faculty of knowing according to intention."
"Furthermore, the mind and toil are both manifestations of the *bodhi* that arise from the exhaustion of staring.
The above summarizes the formation of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) through the conjunction of arising and ceasing.
The objects appearing in dreams exist because of sleep; thus, the "deity" one bows to is merely a fabrication.

Once awakened from sleep, one does not realize that existence is merely provisional; yet, upon reviewing it, one recalls and conceives of it as real—this is called the inverted arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.
Whether awake or asleep, whether remembering or forgetting, all are instances of arising and ceasing.

It is the same within the Dharma: the movement of the mind manifesting objects is already illusory; yet because the *vastu-vijñāna* (the consciousness of things) does not comprehend this, it perceives objects as truly existent, which is called "inversion.
The mutual displacement of object and discrimination, changing from moment to moment, is termed arising, abiding, change, and cessation (*utpāda-sthiti-anyathātva-nirodha*).

Observe that these processes of arising and ceasing all return to the mental faculty (*manas*). As habitual perfuming continues uninterrupted, the moment-to-moment discrimination is what is called the mental faculty.
Both the discriminating mind and the objects discriminated are merely the weary manifestations of ignorance within the nature of awakening.
Second, the absence [of a self] is distinguished in relation to objects:
"Based on the two kinds of delusory objects—arising and ceasing—the aggregate of cognition abides in the center, drawing in and grasping internal objects.
"Aggregate" (*ji*) means to collect.
"Middle" (*zhōng*) refers here to the "internal" (*nèi*). "Inhaling" (*xī*) and "gathering" (*cuō*) both mean to take up.

Through the objects of arising and ceasing, one triggers and accumulates an internal nature of awareness; this awareness constantly takes up arising and ceasing and discriminates internally. This is not the same as the previous five [senses] which illuminate external objects; therefore, they are called "internal objects" (*nèichén*), because the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) internally conditions and does not condition the external. This is what was previously described in the text as "gathering on conditions and shaking within."
"When seeing and hearing flow against the current, such that the flow does not reach the ground, this is called the nature of awakened awareness.
This nature of awakened awareness is ultimately without substance, being detached from those two objects of awakening and sleep, and arising and ceasing."
This distinguishes [this state] from the preceding five.
"Flowing against the current" refers to turning back toward the objects of perception.
"Ground" (bhūmi) means a locus.

The first five [sense organs] only accord with and grasp external objects; they cannot reflexively take internal objects as their conditions. Therefore, these internal objects are termed "the sphere beyond reach.
This sphere beyond reach is conjoined only with the mental faculty (*manas*), and this very point of conjunction constitutes the mental-cognitive faculty (*manovijñānendriya*).
2. Refuting [existence] to establish signlessness, in two parts:
1. Indicating non-arising:
"In this way, Ānanda!"

"You should know that this faculty of awareness does not come from waking or sleeping, nor does it exist through arising and ceasing; it does not emerge from the faculties, nor is it born from emptiness.
Second, the refutation of its place of origin.
"Why is this? If [the dream] arises from waking, then upon falling asleep it immediately ceases; what, then, would constitute sleep?
It must exist while one is awake, yet if it ceases, it becomes non-existent; who then would undergo that cessation?"
If birth arises from extinction, then as extinction ceases, birth would also cease; who then would know the one who is born?

If it emerges from the sense organs, then its two aspects—waking and sleeping—would open and close along with the body. Apart from these two forms, this conscious knower is like a flower in the sky, ultimately devoid of intrinsic nature.
"If it arises from emptiness, it is itself the cognition of emptiness; what concern does it have with your faculty of entry?

First, he uses the analogy of waking and sleeping; next, he uses the analogy of arising and ceasing. Although there are two distinct metaphors, both refute the notion that the object gives rise to cognition, demonstrating that they are mutually present and mutually absent.

Next, I shall refute the claim that [the mind] arises from the sense organs. The mental faculty (*manas*) has no discernible characteristics; it is manifested through the states of waking and sleeping. One knows this to be the mental faculty because one can think and examine while awake, whereas one dreams while asleep.
Now, I refute the notion that waking and sleeping are merely the opening and closing of the body itself, rather than functions of the mental faculty.
The *Liezi* states: "When one awakens, the form opens; when one sleeps, the form merges.
"Merges" (*jiao*) means to unite.
The *Zhuangzi* also says: "In sleep, there is a gathering of mergers; upon awakening, the form opens."

The mind, whether awake or asleep, has no inherent substance; it merely follows along with the body and is not the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) itself. One should know that the mental faculty is ultimately unobtainable.
If it were produced from emptiness, it would likewise be untenable.
3. Conclusion on Falsity:
"Therefore, you should know that the sense-base of the mind (manāyatana) is false; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
3. Refuting the Twelve Bases: This constitutes the correct refutation of the objective spheres.
Part Two:
First, the general inquiry:
"Furthermore, Ānanda!"
"How are the twelve bases (āyatana) fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (tathatā)?
Having already provided a general indication above, [the text] now specifically interrogates them to reveal the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha.
Second, the specific refutation, in six parts:
1. The sense base of the eye and visible forms has three parts:
first, citing an instance to pose a question.
"Ānanda!..."
"You should now observe this Jeta Grove and its various springs and ponds; what do you think?
Do these forms arise first and are then seen by the eye, or does the eye arise first and then perceive the characteristics of form?"

"Place" (sthāna) is defined as the locus of arising; the six sense organs and the six objects are the loci where consciousness arises. Since the organs have already been refuted previously, we now primarily refute the objects; however, since they are refuted by means of their mutual correspondence with the organs, the text asks simultaneously about the arising of form and the arising of the eye, and so forth.
2. Refutation by following the opponent's argument: "Ānanda!

If it were the eye-organ that produced the appearance of form, then when seeing empty space—which is not form—the nature of form would have to dissolve. If it dissolved, then everything would manifest as being utterly non-existent."
"Since the characteristics of form do not exist, who can clarify the substance of emptiness?
Emptiness is likewise so.
This refutes the sense organs, their arising, and their objects.
The first two phrases state the position; the section beginning with "seeing emptiness is not form" refutes the view that there is emptiness within form.
Now, by contrasting form and emptiness, this passage refutes form.
When emptiness is perceived, there is no longer form; since the sense faculties have already produced form, it is called the "nature of form," and thus it should naturally perish.

Once that which produces has perished, how can that which is produced exist? Therefore, it is said that everything manifested is utterly non-existent; this is the manifestation of emptiness and the dissolution of form.
Regarding the characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), there are two meanings:
first, emptiness does not manifest of itself, but is manifested by means of form; now that form is absent, from what would emptiness be manifested?

Furthermore, the sense organs (*indriya*) that are capable of producing [consciousness] are likewise material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*); since the characteristic of form has vanished, the organs also perish accordingly.
Since the sense faculties have already ceased, by what means could one further discern the substance of emptiness?
This indicates that emptiness has no manifest form.
"Emptiness is likewise" serves as an analogy to refute the emptiness of arising; its mode of activity is like that of form.

"If, moreover, the visual consciousness arises from the dust of form, then when one contemplates emptiness—which is not form—the seeing will immediately perish; once it has perished, it is utterly non-existent. Who then would perceive empty space and form?"
This refers to the destruction of the objective sphere (*viṣaya*) and the production of the sense-faculties (*indriya*).
The first two phrases state the proposition; from "contemplating emptiness" (*śūnyatā-darśana*) onwards, it is the refutation.
This also involves a refutation through the mutual opposition of form (*rūpa*) and emptiness; this is the refutation of form.
Since form has already given rise to the sense-faculties, by the time one contemplates emptiness, form has already been extinguished; from what, then, could the faculties arise to perceive emptiness?
Furthermore, form can manifest emptiness, but when emptiness is seen, form has already been extinguished; by whom, then, is emptiness manifested?
The single character "form" (*rūpa*) at the end contains the meaning that emptiness can give rise to seeing; one should know that this applies by analogy to form.
By refuting [the subject] alone, both knots are untied, perfectly exhausting the intent of the translation.
Third, the conclusion indicates their falsity.

"Therefore, you should know that seeing and form are both empty and have no location; thus, the two locations of form and seeing are illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor arising spontaneously."
"Having no location" means having no place of birth.
The rest of the text is self-evident.
Second, the ear and sound base has three parts:
First, citing an event to verify:
"Ānanda! Listen further to this:
when the meal is prepared in this Jeta Grove, the drum is struck; when the assembly gathers, the bell is tolled. The sounds of the bell and drum continue one after another. What do you think?"
"Do these sounds come to the ear, or does the ear go to the place where the sound is?
This refers to the hearing of two sounds, such as those from a bell and a drum, in order to refute the notion of movement between the sense organ and its object.
If one knows that both are equally false and illusory, where would there be going and where would there be coming?
Second, refuting the argument by following its own assumptions: "Ānanda!..."

Furthermore, if this sound comes to the side of the ear, then just as I was begging for alms in Śrāvastī while being at the Jeta Grove, there would be no "I" present; yet this sound must come to Ānanda’s ears. If that were so, Maudgalyāyana and Kāśyapa would not hear it together, let alone the one thousand two hundred and fifty śramaṇas who, upon hearing the bell, all came to the place of the meal at the same time.
"Breaking the sound" refers to its arrival at the locus of the ear.
The first two phrases state the proposition, which is then refuted in the section beginning with "As I...
First, an analogy is presented: "Buddha" refers to the sound.
The city represents the faculty of hearing;
the forest represents the bells and drums.
This sound is refuted by the following examples.
Once the sound has reached your ears, it has already departed from the bell or drum; it should logically be heard by you alone and not be audible to others as well.
Yet this is not the case, for everyone hears it. You should therefore know that the sound has no coming or going.

"If, moreover, your ear were to go to the location of that sound—just as when I return to dwell in the Jeta Grove and am no longer present in the city of Śrāvastī—then when you hear the sound of a drum, your ear would have already gone to the place where the drum is being struck. When the sounds of bells arise simultaneously, you should not be able to hear them all together, let alone the various sounds of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep within them."
"Breaking the ear" refers to proceeding to the locus of sound.
The first two phrases state the premise, which is then refuted in the section beginning with "As I...
First, an analogy is presented: the Buddha is likened to the auditory faculty (*śrotra-indriya*), Jeta Grove to the drum, and Ānanda to the city.
I shall refute this by means of the following analogy:

if the ear-faculty were to travel to the location of the drum, Ānanda would be deprived of his own ear-faculty; thus, when the bell and the drum sound simultaneously, he should not be able to hear the sound of the bell, let alone any other sounds.
"If there is no coming or going, there is likewise no hearing.
This double conclusion establishes that the meaning of "hearing" is not established.
Third, the conclusion demonstrates its falsity.

"Therefore, you should know that hearing and sound both have no location; thus, the two locations of hearing and sound are illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor existing as a spontaneous nature."
3. The sense-base of the nose and odors has three parts:
first, citing a case to pose a question: “Ānanda!
Furthermore, smell this sandalwood in the incense burner; if even one *zhu* of it were burned, its fragrance would be smelled simultaneously throughout the forty *li* within the city of Śrāvastī.
What do you think: does this fragrance arise from the sandalwood tree,
or does it arise from your nose,
or does it arise from space?
In this context, the inquiry concerns only the locus where the object arises; it differs from the preceding section’s refutation through the confrontation of sense-faculties and objects.
Second, the refutation by restating their respective calculations: “Ānanda!...”

Furthermore, if this fragrance were produced in your nose, then as it is produced by the nose, it should emerge from the nose; since the nose is not sandalwood, how could there be the scent of sandalwood within the nose?
"To say that you 'hear' fragrance implies it enters through the nose; yet fragrance issues from within the nose, so to say one 'hears' it is incorrect.
This refutes the arising [of cognition] from the sense organ (*indriya*).
"稱汝" (To say you) restates the opponent's position; "稱鼻" (To say nose) below is the formal refutation (*samyak-dūṣaṇa*); "稱汝" (To say you) below is the concessive refutation (*anujñāta-dūṣaṇa*).

Even if you grant that the nose can produce fragrance, although the sense of "producing" is established, the sense of "smelling" is not established; for it merely emits fragrance and does not receive it from the outside to come into contact with the nose.
"If fragrance were produced from emptiness, and if the nature of emptiness were eternal, then fragrance should be ever-present; why then rely on burning this withered wood in the incense burner?
This refutes the notion that fragrance is produced from emptiness.
If emptiness were permanent, fragrance should be ever-present.
If fragrance were always present, why would it be necessary to burn wood for its scent to be perceived?

"If it were produced from the wood, then this fragrant substance would become smoke through burning; if the nose were to perceive it, it should be enveloped by the smoke. Yet before that smoke has risen far into the air, how is it already smelled within forty li?"
This refutes [the opponent's position] based on the coarse and manifest appearance of the smoke as it is perceived, without taking its subtle essence into account.

If one were to represent it by means of smoke, it would actually be said that [the fire] has not yet reached [it]; therefore, it is stated that "the smoke rises into the air but has not yet traveled far."
The smoke is still nearby, yet its scent is perceived from afar; thus one knows that the fragrance does not emanate from the wood itself.
Third, the conclusion demonstrating its falsity:

"Therefore, you should know that the fragrance, the nose, and the act of smelling all lack a fixed location. Thus, both the act of smelling and the fragrance are false in their two respective locations; fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature."
4. The sense base of the tongue and tastes has three parts:
first, citing a case to pose a question: “Ānanda!
"You regularly carry your alms bowl among the assembly twice a day; during that time, you may encounter ghee, curd, or clarified butter, which are called superior flavors.
What do you think? Does this flavor arise from within the empty sky?"
"Does it arise within the tongue,
or does it arise within the food?
Second, the refutation by addressing each respective calculation.

“Ānanda! If this flavor were produced in your tongue, and there were only one tongue within your mouth, then at that time your tongue would already have become the flavor of ghee. Upon encountering black rock honey, it should not change; if it does not change, it cannot be called ‘knowing flavor. If it does change, then the tongue is not a manifold entity—how then can a single tongue perceive many flavors?”
This refutes the arising from the sense-faculties.
First, the thesis: according to your position, the single tongue below cannot perceive multiple tastes.
If taste were derived from the tongue, there should be no distinction between tastes.
If it does not descend and break [the object], even if you were to grant that taste is not distinguished, since taste would then be undifferentiated, how could there be the cognition of taste?
If it transforms, this refutes the transformation of taste; the tongue would then have multiple entities. The first two lines refute by inversion, while the latter two lines conclude the refutation.
In that case, as the tongue follows after flavors, the tongue would become manifold;
yet this is not so for you, therefore it is asked: "How can many flavors be known by a single tongue?
Furthermore, if [the knowledge] were produced from food, since food is not conscious, how could it know itself?
Furthermore, if the cognition of food were identical to the cognition of another’s food, what would it have to do with your own cognition of names and flavors?
This refutes the arising [of cognition] from the object.

The first three phrases constitute the direct refutation: if flavor were produced by the food itself, it should not depend upon the sense organ; yet without the organ, how could the distinct food itself produce flavor?
If the food were to possess taste, it would have to possess consciousness; if it lacked consciousness, how could it know for itself?

Furthermore, even if the food were to break down as it passes down and you were to grant that the food could know for itself, this would be equivalent to another person tasting a flavor—what connection would that have to the cognition of your own tongue?
"If it were born from emptiness, what flavor would you experience when eating empty space?
If that empty space were to have a salty taste, once your tongue was salted by it, your face would also be salted; then the people of this world would be just like fish in the sea."

"Once one has constantly experienced saltiness, one no longer knows what it is to be bland; if one does not recognize blandness, one is likewise unaware of saltiness. If there is necessarily nothing known, how can it be called 'taste'?
This refutes the notion of "arising from emptiness."
The first three lines cite and examine the [opponent's] position, which will certainly be formally refuted below.

The first four lines state that both the body and the face are salty; the final two lines state that their salinity is identical to that of the ocean’s whirlpools. If they were equally salty, there would be no difference between them and sea fish.

Having already refuted "permanence" above, the first four lines here mutually negate both [permanence and impermanence] so that neither remains. Even if you grant that saltiness is permanent, it ultimately cannot be like sweetness; if there were no sweet taste, how could saltiness be manifested?
Neither the bland nor the salty can be established as stable;
necessarily, the latter two lines conclude that this is not the cognition of taste. Since one cannot distinguish between the salty and the bland, it cannot be called the cognition of taste.
3. Conclusion and Demonstration of Falsity:

"Therefore, you should know that the sense of taste, the tongue, and the act of tasting all lack a fixed location; thus, both tasting and taste are equally false, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor arising spontaneously."
5. The Sense Base of Body Contact, in three parts:
First, citing a fact to pose a question:
"Ānanda, you habitually rub your head with your hand every morning; what do you think about this?"
"Regarding this massage, who is it that performs the touching?
Is it done with the hands, or rather with the head?
Since the standard procedure for massage is always thus, he therefore massaged his head.
This investigation reveals that there are faults in both [theories]: that the faculty of touch resides in the head or that it resides in the hand. These will be refuted below.
Second, the refutation by restating the respective positions:
"If it were in the hand, the head would be devoid of cognition; how, then, could contact be established?"
If [the sense organ] were located in the head, the hand would be useless; how, then, could it be called "contact"?

This refutes [the notion of contact] through mutual presence and mutual absence. Contact is established only when the sense faculty (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*) manifest together; because one exists while the other is absent, it is not called contact.
"If each part were to possess [consciousness] individually, then you, Ānanda, would have two bodies.
This refutes the notion that consciousness exists as two distinct substances.
If the head and hands each possessed [consciousness], there would be two cognitions; with two cognitions, there would consequently be two Ānanda-bodies. Which body, then, would be you?
"If contact were produced by the head and hand meeting as one, then the hand and head would constitute a single entity; if they were a single entity, contact could not be established.
This refutes [the position] by demonstrating that they must form a single entity.
The first four lines constitute the direct refutation: if the head and the hand were to produce a single contact together, it would result in these two distinct entities merging into one.
Even if one were to grant that they become one, contact itself could not be established; this is the conclusion of the refutation.
"If they were two distinct entities, with respect to whom would contact exist?
If it exists in the agent and not the object, or in the object and not the agent, then space should not enter into contact with you."
This refutes the previous defense.
The first two phrases cite that defense and raise a general challenge.
If you offer this defense:
If that which is produced is one while that which produces it is two, how can you claim that my head and hands are not different? In that case, where would this contact of a single entity reside?
Therefore it is said: "With whom does contact reside?

The subsequent two lines, which push the argument forward, refute this in the same manner as before; as previously stated: "If it were located in the hand, then the head would be useless," and so forth.
One should not claim that it arises from the destruction of emptiness; since even dharmas with form cannot arise, how much less could contact be produced from a void that is non-existent?
Third, the conclusion demonstrates its falsity.

"Therefore, you should know that the perception of touch and the body both have no location; thus, both the body and touch are equally illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor arising spontaneously."
6. The sense-base of mind and mental objects has three parts:
first, citing a phenomenon to pose a question:
"Ānanda!..."
Regarding the principles by which the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—which are constantly the objects of your mental consciousness are produced:
do these phenomena arise from the mind itself, or do they exist separately from the mind in some other location?
The phenomena of the three natures (trisvabhāva) that are the objects of mental focus encompass all things exhaustively.
Because they arise spontaneously, they are said to be "generated.
These focal phenomena are either identical to the mind or distinct from it; both positions entail logical fallacies, which will be refuted in the following text.
2. Refutation by following the opponent’s calculation: “Ānanda!
If it were identical to the mind, then dharmas would not be objects; they would not be what the mind takes as its object. How, then, could they constitute a sense-field?”
This refutes that it is the mind itself.
The first phrase restates the position; the second phrase establishes the conclusion; and "it is not the mind" below refutes [the opponent].
Since it is indeed the mind, it is certainly not an external object (*viṣaya*).
If it were not a dust-particle (viṣaya), it would not be an object of perception for the mind; how then could it be called the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana)?
Below, [the text] refutes [the existence of dharmas] apart from the mind:
"If there were a separate location apart from the mind, would the self-nature of dharmas be consciousness or non-consciousness?"
This is a double interrogation based on a restatement of the opponent's position.
The first two phrases constitute the restatement, while the subsequent portion constitutes the interrogation.
Since this phenomenon is already asserted to be separate from the mind, it is further interrogated through the categories of "known" and "unknown" in order to refute it.
"That which knows is called the mind; it is distinct from you yet not an external object, being the same as the mental capacity of others.
It is you, and it is the mind; how could your mind be further divided into two from you?"
This refutes the notion that there is cognition [apart from the mind].
The first phrase negates the established view of the "mind-only" (cittamātra) by stating that if any phenomenon apart from the mind were to possess cognition, it ought to be called "mind.
The subsequent section, beginning with "different from you," further analyzes this difference to refute it; specifically, the first two phrases refute the notion of difference.
If the faculty of cognition were distinct from your mind, it would be identical to that of another person, because it is distinct from your mind yet possesses cognition.

Thus, your [text’s] three subsequent lines refute [the view that cognition] is identical to the mind: the first line and a half restate and establish the premise, while the latter two lines provide the refutation.
Since the faculty of cognition is identical to your own mind, it would follow that there must be another mind outside of your own; therefore, it is said that "there would be two more than you.

If it were not the faculty of cognition, then since this object is neither form, sound, fragrance, flavor, texture, nor the characteristics of separation, union, cold, warmth, or empty space, where could it possibly exist?
"Now, since there is no representation whatsoever of emptiness within form, there should not be an emptiness external to form in the human realm.
Since the mind is not an object of perception, from what could its locus be established?
This refutes ignorance.
The first five phrases establish that it is certainly neither form nor emptiness; the next phrase inquires where it might be.
Since form and emptiness encompass all phenomena exhaustively, if it is neither form nor emptiness, where does it now reside?

Now, regarding the latter two lines, it is inferred that there is nothing to be manifested. If this dharma-object (*dharmāyatana*) were also subsumed within form and emptiness, by what means could one know it to be a dharma-object?

It should not be argued that the latter two lines refute the existence of anything outside of emptiness; for if there is no manifestation within form and emptiness, this object cannot be established as existing outside of emptiness, because emptiness has no exterior.

The first two lines of the verse conclude the meaning of "having no location. As examined above, since the mental object (*dharmāyatana*) does not exist, the mind has no objective sphere to which it could be related; from what, then, could a location be established?
3. Conclusion and Demonstration of Falsity:

"Therefore, you should know that dharmas and the mind both have no location; thus, both the mental faculty and dharmas are equally false, being fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature."
4. Refuting the eighteen elements (dhātus), in two parts:
first, the general inquiry:
"Furthermore, Ānanda!"
"What are the eighteen *dhātus* (realms) that are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness?
*Dhātu* in Sanskrit is translated here as "realm" (*jie*); "realm" carries the meaning of "cause," because the three—sense organ, object, and consciousness—mutually serve as causes for one another.
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of "genus" (*gotra*): the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness each constitutes a single genus.
Moreover, the six [faculties], such as the eye and so forth, are distinct because their genera are different.
Second, the specific refutation has six parts:
1. The visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) has three parts:
first, the restatement of the position followed by a dual inquiry: "Ānanda!..."

As you have clarified, visual consciousness arises with the eye and visible forms as conditions. Does this consciousness arise because of the eye and take the eye as its constituent element (*dhātu*), or does it arise because of visible forms and take visible forms as its constituent element?

In the provisional teachings of the Hīnayāna, the Buddha spoke of the various laws of causes and conditions; now, clarifying the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), he shows that both "causes and conditions" and "spontaneity" are mere conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*). Therefore, he cites these terms here to interrogate them.
2. Refutation by following the opponent's argument: "Ānanda!
If [consciousness] arises dependent on the eye, then in the absence of form and space, there would be nothing to distinguish; even if you possessed such consciousness, what would you use it for?"
"Your perception is neither blue, yellow, red, nor white; since it has no representation, from what could a realm be established?
This refutes the arising of the sense-faculties.
The first phrase restates the position.
Since the latter four propositions do not exist—namely, that there is consciousness without an object—what purpose would there be in refuting them?
If [consciousness] arises from the sense faculties themselves, it does not require an object; yet if its object were absent, what would it distinguish?
Since the object of cognition (*ālambana*) does not exist, what use is there for the subject that cognizes it?
Your observation of the following four lines constitutes the refutation that the sense-faculties (*indriya*), which give rise to consciousness, lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If you claim that the faculties produce [consciousness], yet these faculties are not blue or any other color, they are invisible and lack any manifestation.
If the sense faculties themselves are not established, from what could consciousness arise?
The following refutes the arising [of consciousness] from objects:
"If it arises because of form, then when space is devoid of form, your consciousness should cease; how then can that consciousness know the nature of emptiness?"
"If form undergoes change, you likewise perceive the shifting and transformation of its characteristics; yet if your consciousness does not shift, from what basis could the realms be established?
This refutes the notion that consciousness is destroyed when the characteristics of form and emptiness are overturned.
The first line cites the opponent's position; the subsequent four lines establish the reasoning for the correct refutation.
Since [space] arises from form, when space appears and form perishes, consciousness should likewise cease accordingly; who then would perceive empty space?
If form undergoes change, as stated in the following five phrases, this is a refutation based on principle:

if form is subject to transformation, you must be able to perceive that the fundamental consciousness of transformation does not itself migrate; since there would then be no characteristic of form, from what realm could it be established?
"If it changes along with transformation, the characteristics of the realm would naturally cease to exist.
If it does not change and remains constant, then since it arises from form, it should not be able to perceive the location of empty space."
This refutation of the "element" (dhātu) based on whether it changes or does not change consists of two parts.

The first two phrases refute [the existence of] consciousness by means of its changing: if matter (rūpa) changes when it undergoes transformation, and consciousness likewise changes accordingly, what can be called "consciousness"?

The following four lines refute the position that consciousness is unchanging: if it does not undergo transformation, then consciousness would exist eternally; since it originally arises from form, it ought not to be able to know emptiness.

"If both kinds of eyes and forms were to arise together, then when they combined, they would be separated in the middle; and when they were separated, they would join as two. Their essential natures would thus be confused and disordered; how, then, could they constitute a realm?"
This refutes [the view that consciousness] arises from both [root and object].

If the intermediate element (dhātu) were produced from the conjunction of the sense faculty and the object, then this intermediate element of consciousness would have the distinction of being either cognizant or non-cognizant; therefore, it is said that [consciousness] is distinct from the intermediate element.

If it were established as distinct, then within this consciousness, one half of the element would be conjoined with the faculty and the other half conjoined with the object; thus, it is said to be "conjoined in two ways.

If such twofold conjunction were established, there would be the fault of confusion, because knowing and not-knowing would belong to the same element, and thus the definition of an "element" (dhātu) would be undermined.
Alternatively, "separation" (*li*) means opening up, or it may mean "non-existence.
Third, the conclusion demonstrates their falsity:

"Therefore, you should know that with the eye and forms as conditions, the eye-consciousness element arises; yet these three locations are entirely non-existent. Thus, the eye, forms, and the consciousness element—these three—are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature."
2. The ear and the sound-element: three parts.
First, the restatement of the position and the dual inquiry: “Ānanda!...”

Furthermore, regarding what you have clarified— that the ear and sound serve as conditions to produce auditory consciousness— does this consciousness arise because of the ear and take the ear as its constituent element (dhātu),
or does it arise because of sound and take sound as its constituent element?
2. Refutation by following the specific calculation: "Ānanda!

If [hearing] were produced from the ear, then when the two characteristics of movement and stillness are not present before it, the faculty would fail to constitute cognition, and there would necessarily be nothing known."
"If even cognition itself is not established, what form or appearance could consciousness have?
This first statement refutes the arising of the sense organs; this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The first phrase restates the premise, while the subsequent three phrases—beginning with "movement and stillness"—properly refute that which gives rise [to the sense organs].
If there were no external objects, the sense organs themselves could not be established, because it is through the presence of an object that cognition is triggered.
This necessarily refutes the notion of [an organ] producing [cognition]; for if there were truly no cognition, the organ itself would not even stand, so how could there be consciousness?

"If one takes the ear as the hearer, since there is neither motion nor stillness, hearing would have no basis for establishment. How then could the ear-organ, along with visible forms and tactile objects, be called the element of consciousness?
Furthermore, from what would the element of ear-consciousness itself be established?"
This refutes the "dust-like" ear.

The first three phrases refute by concession: even if one were to concede that the physical ear-organ which perceives the dust-like objects has the capacity to hear, if there is neither motion nor stillness, hearing itself cannot be established.
How are the latter three phrases a formal refutation? How can these visible, superficial, and variegated objects of touch and form be considered the "element" (dhātu) of consciousness?
Furthermore, the two subsequent lines pose a dual inquiry regarding the two sense organs: from what element do the ear-consciousness and the others arise?
"If consciousness were produced from sound and existed because of sound, it would have no relation to hearing.
Without hearing, the locus of the characteristic of sound would cease to exist.
The following section refutes production from the object.
The first phrase restates the position; the subsequent section refutes it by demonstrating that consciousness, its cause, and both the faculty and the object are simultaneously non-existent.
If sound can produce consciousness, why depend upon hearing? This refutes the existence of the faculty.
If the faculty does not exist, then sound likewise does not exist; this refutes the existence of the object.
If both the sense faculty and the object are absent, from what would consciousness arise?
[The opponent replies: "Consciousness arises from sound. [The Master asks: "If you grant that sound exists because of hearing, then hearing should also hear the consciousness."
"Upon hearing the sound, consciousness is simultaneously refuted.

The first three phrases present two simultaneous propositions: you claim that consciousness arises because of the sound, yet you also admit it exists because of the sense organ. Now, at the very moment of hearing the sound, it is precisely the hearing-consciousness [that is perceived]."
"If there is no hearing, there is no constituent element (*dhātu*); if there is hearing, it is identical to sound.
The first phrase refutes the absence of a constituent element when there is no hearing.
If there is no hearing, consciousness does not hear, nor does sound; thus, both the faculty of hearing and the object heard lack the meaning of a constituent element.
The final phrase, "hearing-consciousness is simultaneously destroyed along with sound," can be understood.
"Since consciousness has already been heard, who knows this hearing-consciousness?
This establishes that there is nothing capable of refutation.
The consciousness that is able to cognize has already made the heard object its domain; who then is the knower that knows this hearing-consciousness?
"If there were no knower, it would ultimately be like grass and wood."
"Since there is no cognition, grasses and trees are [mere] destruction.
Since discernment (*vijñapti*) is absent, how do grasses and trees differ?

It should not be that the Śrāvakas' realms are intermingled to form a middle realm; since there is no middle position among the realms, from what could the characteristics of internal and external arise?"
This refutes the notion of co-arising.

The first two lines directly refute the intermediate realm (*madhyama-dhātu*); since it is not even possible for the sense organ (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*) to arise individually, how could there be such a principle for them to arise together?

The final three lines demonstrate the non-existence of the organ and the object: the "middle" is established in contrast to the "extremes"; since the middle is not established, the extremes cannot be established either.
3. Conclusion showing their falsity:

"Therefore, you should know that the ear, sound, and the auditory consciousness-element arise with these as conditions; yet these three locations are entirely non-existent. Thus, the triad of the ear, sound, and the auditory element are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of spontaneous nature."
3. The Nose-Consciousness Element has three parts:
first, the restatement of the position followed by a dual inquiry: "Ānanda!..."

Furthermore, regarding what you have clarified: when the nose and fragrance serve as conditions to produce nose-consciousness, does this consciousness arise because of the nose and take the nose as its constituent element (*dhātu*), or does it arise because of the fragrance and take the fragrance as its constituent element?
He refuted each of these calculations in turn: "Ānanda!
If it arises because of the nose, then within your mind, what constitutes the 'nose'?"
"Is it by taking on the form of flesh with its two claws, or is it by taking on the nature of smelling, knowing, and moving?
First, he refutes the arising from the sense organs; here, he asks about both the physical (floating dust) and the ultimate (supreme meaning) organs, and in both cases there are faults.
"If one takes the physical form as the basis, then the fleshly substance is the body; the cognition of the body is contact.
To call it 'body' is not to call it 'nose'; to call it 'contact' is to designate it as an object. Since even the 'nose' has no inherent name, how can one establish a constituent element (dhātu)?"
This refutes the superficial dust.
The first phrase restates the position; the following two phrases refute it.
If one were to grasp both claws, this would be subsumed under the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and would not belong to the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*).
If there were such a thing as cognition, it would only be called "cognition of touch" and not "cognition of fragrance.
The two phrases following "name-body" (nāmakāya) conclude that [the nose] is not fragrance. The phrase "the nose itself...
below points to the meaning of the absence of a [distinct] element (*dhātu*).
Below this, the supreme sense organs are refuted:
"If you take olfactory cognition as the basis, then what within your mind constitutes that which knows?
If you claim the flesh constitutes the knower, then the cognition of the flesh is fundamentally tactile and not olfactory."
The first three phrases cite the opponent's position and pose a general question, which is then refuted by the subsequent discussion on "flesh.
The "floating dust" (sensory objects) is that which is known; the body itself knows the touch, and it is not the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*).

"If you take emptiness to be consciousness, then since emptiness is not the body, the flesh would not be conscious. If this were so, then emptiness would be you and your body would not be consciousness; in that case, Ānanda, you should have no location today."
The "shattering of emptiness" is knowledge.

The first three phrases shatter the roots of ignorance and lack of perception; likewise, the following two phrases represent the shattering of the body as emptiness itself; and the final three phrases below conclude that there is no fundamental substance to your body.
"If fragrance constitutes cognition, then that cognition belongs to the fragrance itself; what concern is it to you?
To refute the notion that fragrance is cognition is precisely the point of this refutation.
Fragrance possesses its own cognition; what does it have to do with your nose?
"If fragrant and foul odors must arise from your nose, then those two kinds of flowing air—fragrance and stench—would not arise from the *eranda* (Ilan) tree or the sandalwood tree.
This refutes the shifting argument.

The first two phrases cite the opponent's position: "Suppose you were to say that they are not unrelated because there exists a self and a nose, and only through these can fragrance and stench be established—just as the olfactory faculty exists because of fragrance. This is then refuted in the following passage.
Now, I shall examine this with four propositions to refute the notion that fragrance is produced.
"Since the two substances do not come here, when you smell your own nose, is it fragrant or foul?
By smelling the organ itself, what scent is there to be refuted?
"If it is foul, it is not fragrant; if it is fragrant, it should not be foul.
Fragrance and foulness exclude and negate one another.
It is not that they do not exist; it is simply that there is no simultaneous perception of both.

"If you were able to smell both fragrance and stench simultaneously, then you, as a single person, would have two noses; or, as there are two Ānandas here questioning me, which of the two would be your true self?"
Thus, both [theories] are refuted by the fact that two entities cannot coexist.
If the nose were to produce fragrance, it would necessarily not smell odors;
if it were to produce odors, it should necessarily not smell fragrance.
Now that both have been heard, the nose must possess two [aspects].
If two noses were established, two distinct entities would result; what, then, would constitute the true entity?

"If the nose were one, there would be no duality between fragrance and stench. If stench were already fragrance, and fragrance were further stench, then these two natures would not exist; from whom, then, could the realms be established?"
Thus, both [the nose and its objects] simultaneously vanish, which is their refutation.
If you do not allow that the nose has two [aspects], then fragrance and stench would be indistinguishable and entirely without differentiation, because they both issue from a single nose.
If there were no fragrance or stench, how could one say that "knowledge arises" or speak of the element of consciousness?

"If [consciousness] arises because of fragrance, and consciousness exists because of fragrance, then just as the eye has the capacity for seeing yet cannot see itself, so too, because it exists because of fragrance, it should not know the fragrance."
The following section refutes the arising [of consciousness] from an object.
The first phrase restates [the opponent's position]; the subsequent five phrases cite examples to refute it by negation.
The eye is capable of seeing, yet seeing does not perceive the eye.
Fragrance can give rise to consciousness, yet consciousness does not know fragrance.
If it knows it, it is not "arising"; if it does not know it, it is not "consciousness.
Fragrance does not exist through knowing; thus, the realm of fragrance is not established.
"Consciousness does not know fragrance; because it depends on the element [of fragrance], it is not established from fragrance.
This is a refutation through successive concessions.
Even if we were to concede that your consciousness can know fragrance, it would be improper to say that it arises from fragrance; therefore, it is said that "if it knows, it is not born [from it]."
If one cannot discern this fragrance or its foulness, how can it be called "consciousness" (vijñāna) or "discernment" (prativijñapti)?
Therefore, it is said that not knowing [the object] is not consciousness.

Since fragrance does not exist apart from the sense organ, there would be no fragrance-element (gandha-dhātu); thus, it is said that fragrance does not exist through cognition, and the fragrance-element is not established.
Consciousness does not perceive fragrance; it cannot be said that consciousness exists because of fragrance.
"Since there is no intermediate state, neither 'internal' nor 'external' can be established; therefore, the nature of hearing is ultimately illusory."
This concludes the refutation.
Since consciousness is without arising, the sense organs and their objects are not established; even if there were such a thing as the nature of hearing, it would all be illusory.
Third, this concludes by demonstrating its illusoriness.

"Therefore, you should know that with the nose and fragrance as conditions, the nose-consciousness element arises; yet in all three locations, these are entirely non-existent. Thus, the triad of the nose, fragrance, and the fragrance-element have from the beginning neither causal conditions nor an inherent nature."
4. The tongue-consciousness element has three parts:
first, the citation of the calculation and the dual inquiry: “Ānanda!...”

Furthermore, regarding what you have clarified— that tongue-consciousness arises with the tongue and flavors as conditions— does this consciousness arise because of the tongue and take the tongue as its constituent element (dhātu),
or does it arise because of flavors and take flavors as its constituent element?
2. Refuting the position by addressing each specific hypothesis: "Ānanda!

If [taste] were produced dependent on the tongue, then all the sugar cane, sour plums, yellow myrobalan, rock salt, fine pepper, ginger, and cassia in the world would have no taste at all; you yourself could then taste your own tongue to see whether it is sweet or bitter."
This refutes the arising from the sense-faculties.

The first phrase restates the premise; the subsequent lines raise the question of the tongue-faculty in the absence of the five flavors, which is to say, the question of whether the tongue can taste itself in the absence of flavor.
"If the nature of the tongue were suffering, who would come to taste it?
The tongue does not taste itself; what, then, could be the cognizer?
If the nature of the tongue were not suffering, flavor would not arise of its own accord; how, then, could the sense-sphere be established?"
This is refuted by the consideration of existence and non-existence.
If the tongue possessed taste, the sense organ itself would have already become the object; who then would know the organ?
When there is no taste, the object of taste must arise [externally]; how then could your organ alone produce consciousness?
Next, [the argument] refutes [the claim that consciousness] arises from the object:

"If consciousness were produced by the taste, then consciousness itself would be the taste; being identical to the tongue faculty, it should not be able to taste itself. How, then, could consciousness discern whether something is a taste or not a taste?"
This citation refutes [the objection] based on ignorance.
Since [taste] arises from flavor, how could it appropriately be called "consciousness"?
Therefore, it is said that consciousness itself constitutes the flavor.
Even if one were to concede that it is called "consciousness," it still does not taste itself; this can be seen by citing an analogy.
Furthermore, all tastes are not produced from a single substance; since tastes arise from many sources, consciousness would consequently have multiple entities.

Just as the five flavors previously mentioned each produce a distinct object, consciousness must likewise arise from its objects and thus possess multiple entities; that is, since consciousness arises from the flavors, consciousness itself becomes manifold.

"If the substance of consciousness were a single unity, its substance would necessarily be of a single flavor; when salty, bland, sweet, and pungent flavors combine and arise together, all their various changing characteristics would become one and the same flavor, and there should be no differentiation between them."
If discrimination is absent, it cannot be called consciousness; how then can it be called the "consciousness-element of tongue and taste"?
Furthermore, if a single entity of consciousness must arise from an object, then the object that gives rise to it should also be a single entity; why then distinguish five separate types?
If one analyzes this, it would follow that [the flavors] are destroyed; since the five flavors would not be distinguished, how could they be called "discriminating" and designated as consciousness?
In that case, the flavor would derive from the consciousness, and the flavor itself should have no distinct existence.

Regarding each of the following phrases, they collectively refute that the substance of consciousness is named after either of two [sources], because it would incur the error of being produced by both the sense organ and the object.
"It should not be that empty space produces your mind-consciousness."
This refutes production from emptiness.
"The union of the tongue and flavors is, within that very state, originally devoid of self-nature; how, then, could an element (dhātu) be produced?
This refutes production from both [self and other]. Since it is produced from their union, to whom does the self-nature belong such that it is called an "element"?
3. Conclusion and Demonstration of Falsity:

"Therefore, you should know that with the tongue and flavors as conditions, the realm of tongue-consciousness arises; yet these three locations are entirely non-existent. Thus, the triad of the tongue, flavors, and the realm of tongue-consciousness are fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they of spontaneous nature."
5. The body and the element of tangibles: three parts.
First, the restatement of the thesis and the dual inquiry: "Ānanda!..."

Furthermore, regarding what you have clarified— that body-contact serves as a condition for the arising of body-consciousness— does this consciousness arise because of the body and take the body as its constituent element (*dhātu*),
or does it arise because of contact and take contact as its constituent element?
2. Refutation by following the opponent's reasoning:

"Ānanda! If [consciousness] were produced because of the body, there would necessarily be no conditions for the two types of mental application—conjunction and separation; what, then, would the body perceive?"
This refutes [the notion that consciousness] arises from the sense organ.

It examines the relationship of mutual dependence; since there is no duality of what is perceived, they serve as conditions through mutual dependence. Thus, it is illogical for this body-organ alone to give rise to consciousness.
Below, [the text] refutes [the notion that consciousness] arises from the object.
"If [cognition] were produced by contact, there would necessarily be no body for you; who then could possess a non-body that knows union and separation?
This refutes the notion of a non-sentient body.
If there is a body but no contact, cognition is not yet established; if there is contact but no body, it cannot be sentient awareness.
It is not the body; it is the absence of a body.
This is the mutual negation and destruction of the lower faculties and their objects. "Ānanda!
"Objects do not possess the cognition of touch; it is the body that knows there is touch.
This points to the principle of direct manifestation.
Objects lack the cognition that perceives touch, whereas the body is able to perceive touch; this principle is luminous and clearly visible.
"To know the body is itself contact; to know contact is itself the body.
The following section refutes this through reasoning.

These two lines indicate that the faculty (the body) and its object (contact) are mutually identical. Now, if you concede that contact can produce consciousness, then contact must possess cognition; how would it differ from the body?
One should be able to say that the body is also called "contact" (*spraṣṭavya*) and contact is also called "body," because both possess cognition.
One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
Your sense-faculty of the body (*kāyendriya*) is necessarily subsumed under contact, because it possesses cognition, just like the contact you yourself maintain.
